Mr. MACKENZIE KING.-that there is any uncertainty as to which party commands the confidence of the electors, then I would feel it necessary to ask His Excellency to summon parliament immediately in order to decide that question before any representation of Canada was made at the conferences. I do not believe that any other course would meet with the approval of hon. gentlemen opposite; certainly in such circumstances no other course would enable an administration to say that it had a mandate from the electors to represent Canada at the conferences. If we are to provide for that possible contingency it must be remembered that it takes something like forty days after the day of polling at a general election before the last of the [DOT]writs is likely to be returned; at least some such length of time has been the period in the past. It would in case of uncertainty take a day or two after the elections to know what the final result would be, and in case of any uncertainty as I have just said there would be the necessity of summoning parliament. Then there would be the time required for the procedure essential to the opening of parliament, and the time likely to be involved in the discussion which would 'follow, and in any such contingency I venture to say it will prove impossible, unless we prorogue to-morrow night, to have Canada represented at the conferences in September. If we are to have the elections on August 11, then it must be understood that in the event of there being any uncertainty in the results, parliament will be reconvened, but equally that there can be no representation of Canada at the conferences until they are well under way with their proceedings.

These facts can be verified for themselves by hon. gentlemen. I have brought this matter before the house because I realize that hon. gentlemen opposite have it in their .power to prevent prorogation to-morrow night. I wish to be scrupulously fair in this matter. The government has no desire to withhold discussion on any of the estimates. As I stated a few days ago, the estimates have been before parliament for two or three months and if there are any features which hon. members wish to have discussed, the government will bring those forward immediately so that they will not be left until the last minute. The government is prepared to bring forward the estimates for the purposes of discussion, in any order which my hon. friend and the leader of the Progressive group (Mr. Gardiner) may suggest. We shall do that in order to ensure that matters in which hon. members are specially interested shall

'be discussed at once. While I realize that there may not be an opportunity for the full discussion which hon. members might desire should take place, it must be agreed that the present situation is a little different from what would apply to any other session of parliament. The government has it within its power to carry the estimates, and I think they 'will be carried no matter how long we take in discussion. If my hon. friend should be 'returned to power, I am sure that he will be Very glad that we have earned them because 'he will find they are all necessary. However, the opportunity will be afforded for the next few months of discussion before the people, and I think that that should serve any purpose which would be served by additional discussion here.

Let me repeat, as a government we are, as respects the dates of prorogation and of the elections, in the hands of hon. gentlemen opposite. If we cannot conclude to-morow night, then the elections will take place, I hope not later than August 11, but certainly not before that date. If we prorogue tomorrow night, the intention of the government is to ask His Excellency for an immediate dissolution of parliament and to have the elections on July 28.

In the preparation of the supplementary estimates the administration has been careful to endeavour to exercise economy and discretion in what we have recommended to the house. It will be seen that care has been taken not to include items which might be regarded as having been included for political purposes. We have tried to keep the supplementary estimates as to purposes and amounts in a form which would commend itself to the house generally. Let me repeat, if any arrangement is to be arrived at as between the different parties in the house it can only b by cooperation on the part of all. In so far as the government is concerned we will do all that is within our power to further that cooperation.

BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):,Leader of the Official Opposition,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,ORDERS WITHDRAWN-EXPEDITING BUSINESS IN ANTICIPATION OP PROROGATION AND ELECTIONS,,Mr. Speaker, I was quite content to make the observations I desire to make after you left the chair, but I rose only to say that I proposed to make a few remarks. The Prime Minister in his observations this afternoon indicated that a situation had been reached when we should decide whether the estimates that are before the house should be carefully and faithfully considered in detail or we should endeavour to secure prorogation by to-morrow night in order that dissolution may follow and a general election be held on the 28th of July. I cannot but think it desirable under our form of government that every possible opportunity should be taken by those who constitute an opposition or who sit in opposition to a government, to analyse its expenditures for the purpose of ascertaining just what the administration proposes to do with the money raised by the taxation of the people of the country. It is idle to say that on the hustings there can be a discussion of the causes for the expenditures. It is because of this fact that when supply is being granted, we ask questions, sometimes embarrassing for those who have to answer, for the purpose of ascertaining just how the country's business is being transacted. We can do that only in supply as our institution now exists. The right hon. gentleman, in his all-too-brief, but what let us hope, will be more extended, experience in opposition, will remember that he regarded it as important that he should study expenditures and criticize the attitude of administrations with respect to them. That after all, has been the duty of an opposition since the party system first began to develop. In other words, with the airing of grievances preceding supply, when the house goes into committee of supply for the purpose of determining what expenditures shall be made, it has a right to inquire and usually does inquire with great care as to how the money is proposed to be spent. That opportunity will not be afforded to the house if it prorogues to-morrow night.

On the other hand, as the Prime Minister has said, there may be in each of the departments certain large contemplated expenditures about which it may be possible to obtain information. I think the Prime Minister has, perhaps with some reluctance, reduced the demands in the supplementary estimates of those who sit behind him. At least, knowing human nature as I do, I think it would be very strange if he had not, and I can readily understand he experienced some difficulty in that regard, for the supplementary estimates, although amounting to $11,000,000, of which $2,500,000 represents a number of

items from the Auditor General's report and governor general warrants, have been reduced by, I should think, about 500 per cent from what the hon. gentleman was asked to accede to. To that extent he has endeavoured to reduce to a minimum the causes for discussion and dispute.

I am not unmindful of the fact that business is in some respects dislocated during a period of a general election, but that is usually so when elections are held in days of buoyant revenues and large favourable balances of trade. Under existing conditions, however, which have been brought about by my hon. friends opposite, a little more difficulty in business because of an election will perhaps not be so perceptible. At any rate I think that is so. While we desire, as I have said, to criticize many of these items; while in fact there is one department alone regarding which I think the public interest would be well served if we took a week in discussing its estimates; in view of the position taken by the administration; in view of the provisions of the Elections Aot necesit&ting a contest being held on a Monday-the aot might have been amended if it had been done early enough, but certainly it could not be amended as the matter stands now because the whole machinery of the act is predicated upon an election being held on a given day of the week and all the computations of time are made from that date-in view of the possible effect upon business, and in view of the very earnest desire there is on this side of the house that this administration should be replaced at the earliest possible moment, we will continue to the best of our ability to expedite the business of the country; and unless some unforeseen circumstance arises or some revelations of startling Character appear when the ministers indicate what they propose to do with the people's money, we shall be glad to assist the government in bringing about the prorogation of parliament tomorrow. That is -the best that we can do under the circumstances.

I think that the right hon. gentleman will say that since we first discussed the matter we have endeavoured to the best of our ability to expedite the business of this parliament. We had hoped that by so doing there would be a greater opportunity afforded
Business of the House

for the discussion of the estimates; but I warn hon. gentlemen opposite that if they go to their constituencies and say that the opposition have acceded to all the expenditures that the government proposed, unnecessary though some of them may be, they will be confronted with the observations of their own Prime Minister this afternoon, who indicated that discussion of the estimates in detail would not be possible if dissolution of this parliament were to take place to-morrow. So choosing, as we do, dissolution rather than detailed discussion of the estimates, we will to the best of our ability assist in bringing about that end.

I do not know that I can usefully add anything further except to say that the views of those who sit to your left, Mr. Speaker, and who a few short weeks ago expressed their earnest desire for an early opportunity to present to the people of this country their views upon political matters, have been greatly confirmed by what has transpired since in their opinion of the insincerity and instability of the administration, and hope that the people may have an early opportunity to pronounce judgment upon a body of men who are no longer fit to govern the country.

^ Mr. ROBERT GARDINER (Acadia): Mr. Speaker, I have taken the opportunity of consulting with my colleagues with regard to the possibility of proroguing to-morrow. In view of the fact that the date of the Imperial conference had been set, I think it would have been better if the Prime Minister had called parliament earlier; for we were two weeks later in meeting this year than in recent years. There was also the possibility of an election before the Imperial conference, and in view of those circumstances it might have been better not to have had such a long recess at Easter. Remembering also that this house has accented the proposal from this comer that some of the more important estimates should go to a committee of this house, a lot of the time of the house might have been saved if the wishes of the house in that respect had been carried out this session, and an opportunity would then have been given to discuss the more important estimates thoroughly. There are a few items in the estimates which my colleagues wish to discuss, but in view of the statements of the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition, I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that we shall do our best to expedite the business of the house so that we may prorogue to-morrow.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Felix Patrick Quinn,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a3f7af51-7840-4658-9556-225a76696410&Language=E&Section=ALL
910908,ca.proc.d.1930-05-29.15.1.26,1930-05-29,2a8c7330-53c3-44dc-9f77-c16aa6af7898,ca.m.2417,Mr. BOURASSA:,,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,ORDERS WITHDRAWN-EXPEDITING BUSINESS IN ANTICIPATION OP PROROGATION AND ELECTIONS,,Oh yes. I am in the happy position that I can speak in the name of the leader of my party, in the name of the whip and of all the inside and outside supporters. I can therefore always express the unanimous opinion of this party to you, Mr. Speaker.

There is a good deal in what the leader of the progressive party (Mr. Gardiner) has said. Everybody knew that there was to be an Imperial conference this fall. Everybody expected that there was to be a general election this year. I therefore agree with the leader of the progressive group that the government might have called parliament at an earlier date. On previous occasions I have pointed out the habit which governments, in this and other countries, but especially in this free and democratic country, have developed of late years of deciding matters altogether according to their own individual convenience without consulting the desire of parliament or even of the country. On the other hand, I agree with the three single gentlemen that the people are expecting at this juncture to have a dissolution of parliament as early as possible, and to have the political situation settled by an expression of public opinion. It has been stated that this parliament should be dissolved now in order that our delegates might go to the Imperial conference with a popular mandate behind them. That is the most serious reason, I think. On the other hand, it should be made clear once for all that the desirability of meeting the representatives of other portions of the British Empire at the Imperial conference should not come before the interests of this country. The first duty of the government is to the parliament of Canada, and the first duty of the parliament of Canada is to the people of Canada. Especially with such a program as we have, I think it would have been useful for the people
Supply-National Revenue

to have had a more thorough examination both of the budget and of the estimates, and especially of the budget. But let that pass. I think we should do our best to make it possible to prorogue to-morrow in order that we may have an election in the month of July. At the same time it should be made quite clear that the manner in which the estimates are voted in this house is entirely unsatisfactory, and whatever party is in power after this election, I hope that some means will be taken to prevent hours and days and weeks of discussion of trivial matters, and then the voting of millions of dollars in a few hours under the pretence that we are in a hurry and that this matter or that matter which is entirely outside the necessities of the situation demand an immediate decision. Parliament is primarily constituted to vote subsidies, and the primary duty of members of parliament is to examine eveiy item in the estimates so as to be able to render an account to the people they represent and to the people of Canada at large. I rose, and it is not the first time since I have been in this parliament, to protest against the manner in which the money of the people, because after all it is the people who pay for these expenditures, is disposed of by their representatives who are supposed to be here to look after the public interest.

910965,ca.proc.d.1930-05-29.18.14,1930-05-29,17d9fbdf-1bc5-4137-ac59-4e782464990f,ca.m.4762,Mr. ROSS (Kingston):,,PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH,,,I have still another complaint. Perhaps the minister may not be responsible for this one, but at least he can bring it to the attention of the Board of Pension Commissioners. There is a great neglect of orphans. The position is this, that once an orphan reaches the age of sixteen he is immediately struck off the pension list, although there is a regulation which provides that if that orphan is attending college or going to school the pension may be continued. I think before the orphan is struck off the list some investigation Should be made. I know children who have practically had to leave school because the mother did not know this regulation was in the act. I think it would be only a small favour to grant that before a child is struck off the list the question should be asked whether or not that child is attending school, and if the child is attending school the pension should be continued. There are cases where the father has been killed and the mother dies and leaves one or two children. I think it is the duty of the Board of Pension Commissioners to look up these cases and see how they are provided for. I have come across three cases where no care was taken; the children were simply struck off and had to be cared for in one case by an aunt and in another by an uncle. I think it is only a very small thing that before these orphans are struck off the list, the department or the Board of Pension Commissioners should look them up, and I submit that suggestion without any further remarks.

Then there is another and perhaps rather more serious complaint about which I am sure the minister has knowledge. There is a situation at present down at the Plaza building where a certain employee is making use of his position there for political purposes. I have had three cases where applicants for pensions have come here, and as they made their applications and came into the other office, they fell into the hands of this employee who said, ''Here, you put your case in the hands of the defeated Liberal candidate, and he will see that you get your pension."" I want to say, Mr. Chairman, that this is going on openly to-day, and I am sure the minister knows the person who is doing it. It is well known to employees of the department and if the minister cares to have us do so we will give him the names of the applicants and the particulars of the case referred by this official to his Liberal friends. We are trying to keep out of this thing; we have a committee which deals with that work and Which is non-political, but the sooner the minister gets rid of an official of this kind the better for himself and for the country.

I quite agree with my hon. friend that there is no reason why the commissioners should not make inquiry as to the condition of the children.

about two hours of the time of the committee in discussing these health matters, but that not being possible, I would refer the minister to page 83 of the report where certain references are made to radium, as follows: The unusual and striking properties of radium as well as its use for the treatment of certain forms of cancer, have resulted in somewhat exaggerated notice having been given it in the daily press. For some years after its romantic discovery great hopes -were held that a wonderful therapeutic agent had been given to the medical profession and a trial was made of radium in an immense variety of diseases. During this period enthusiastic workers
Supply-Pensions and National Health

announced wonderful results. Subsequently, and in the light of properly controlled clinical trials, the bulk of the results were negatived and at the present time the use of radium is severely limited.
The minister admits that he is primarily responsible for that statement which is at variance with the established medical practice of the present time. The report continues:
It is also better known now that radium is dangerous .and should only be used clinically, by specially trained radiologists.

On March 17th I had the honour of introducing a resolution asking for the nationalization of the supply of radium. Unfortunately, only a limited time was available in which to discuss that subject, but we were able to discover that the minister and his government apparently have very little interest in the public health of this country so far as the use of radium is concerned in the treatment of people afflicted with cancer. Shortly after this resolution was introduced, along about the last of April, Doctor Ellice McDonald of the Dupont cancer research institute, University of Pennsylvania, recommended to the American congress practically the identical method of handling radium and cancer cases that had been proposed to this house under the resolution referred to. I would recommend to the minister that he investigate this subject a little more fully. After July 28th next I am sure that we will have a government and a department of health which will give a little more attention to the needs of the public as far as health matters are concerned.

As regards our later convictions, we have been fairly successful in securing long term sentences. It was difficult in the earlier stages to get the magistrates to commit these people for long terms. On the 31st March, 1930, there were in the Westminster penitentiary 82 traffickers, many for five years and some for seven years. As stated in the 1929 annual report, whereas in the preceding year the number of cases in which the option of a fine was given largely exceeded those in which there was none, in 1928-29 the situation was reversed, and 240 of the 430 convictions resulted in gaol sentences in that year; one of seven years, eleven of five years, four of four years, eight of three years, nine of two years, and twenty-eight of one year and over. A day or two ago I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) whether bovine tuberculosis came within his sphere or within the Department of Public Health, and he answered that both departments dealt with it. Therefore my remarks will apply not only to the national health department but also to the agriculture department. I cannot attempt to go into this question at the length I intended owing to the exigencies of time. I assume the Minister of Health has read the report of the Minister of Agriculture. If so, he read that in the province of Quebec 18 to 19 per cent of the cattle of some areas were found to be affected with bovine tuberculosis, while only 2 per cent of the cattle examined in other parts of the Dominion were found to be suffering from this disease. The records of the last seventeen years show that in no other area on this north American continent has the examination of cattle for bovine tuberculosis shown any approach to 18 or 19 per cent of the cattle diseased, with the exception of a small area in the District of Columbia. If the minister viewed this matter from a national standpoint, surely he would be alarmed at the situation in Quebec. In the year 1928, 23,000 cattle in Quebec have been found to be affected with bovine tuberculosis, and were slaughtered. This phenomenal condition cost the country $750,000 last year. The minister

knows there must be some explainable reason for this condition, and he should ask the National Research Council to investigate and report to parliament the causes. It may be due to bad housing of the cattle, if the condition exists at all. I do not believe it does exist, because I am satisfied in my mind that our method of tracing this disease is inferior to that followed by other advanced countries. The work is being done in a slipshod way, but I have not the time to go into that now. Bovine tuberculosis is communicated to man, and has resulted in many of the children of Canada being affected by bone, pulmonary and nodular tuberculosis. This appalling situation ought to arouse the concern and active interest of the Minister of National Health. When we bring his attention to this serious condition of affairs he tells us that the British North America Act has assigned health matters to the various provinces. I want to break down that theory that national health is confined to the jurisdiction of the provinces. Cases and conditions such as these, should surely convince anybody that we ought to have a national health policy.

I wrote the agriculture department of the province of Quebec and asked them whether they had examined any cattle in the province for bovine tuberculosis, and they told me they had been doing it for the last ten years, and in that period had examined 375,000 cattle, and the highest percentage affected was only 3 per cent. Contrast this percentage with the 18 to 19 per cent stated to have been discovered by the federal Department of Agriculture. These contradictory figures naturally *make us question whether this department is actually prepared to carry on its work. I say to the Minister of Agriculture that the research council should convince him and convince Canada as to the peculiar causes which obtain and which bring about such a staggering result. The minister should have his department checked up. I have asked how many men they have in the department whose duty it is to go out and examine the cattle, and they have given me five or six names. I have asked the officials connected with the United States government how many experts they used to examine the cattle in that country and I find where in this country we would have .nine they would have ninety.

We are all familiar with the policy which was introduced in 1927 wherein we decided that rather than try to check people coming into this country who were not physically or mentally fit we would place our own officers in Great Britain and on the continent of Europe to make examinations at certain points. I do not think there is any medical man in the house, or for that matter, in the country, who believes the Department of National Health has been functioning as such a department should function in Canada to-day. The greatest asset we have, after all, is the health and happiness of our people, and surely there should be some arrangement whereby the federal Department of Health, could, as has been said so ably by the hon. member for Kingston city, cooperate with the provincial health departments and help to coordinate the work. Unfortunately, disease does not stop at provincial boundaries and, moreover, it is not confined by the limitations of the British North America Act. If, under the provisions of the British North America Act, the department is not able to cooperate with the provincial health authorities, the Department of National Health has no reason for existing.

I woidd suggest that the minister call a conference of the medical departments of the different provinces and see whether some working arrangement cannot be devised whereby his department can cooperate fully with the provincial health departments.

911201,ca.proc.d.1930-05-29.20.17,1930-05-29,3e478f06-ec31-4aa2-afb1-2c41dbd6f925,ca.m.9413,Mr. MALCOLM:,Minister of Trade and Commerce,DEPARTMENT OP TRADE AND COMMERCE,,,I would like to speak on this item, because it involves the question relative to medical services brought up by
Supply-Trade and Commerce

my hon. friend. In the Department of Trade and Commerce we maintain a service which costs $119,000. This service covers a warehouse at St. Catharines, of which Mr. Corkery is in charge. He collects the various fruit exhibits and puts them up in glass jars for the various Canadian exhibitions. We maintain offices at London, England, with a staff of four people. In Winnipeg there is a staff engaged in the collection of grains, seeds and other cereal products. In the collection of exhibits we spend about $50,000. During the past we have exhibited at state fairs in the United States of America. These samples have also been exhibited in Great Britain; I might say that the cost in connection with all these exhibitions has amounted to about $54,000. Exhibits have also been placed in all the windows of the immigration offices on the continent, in Europe and in the United States. The major portion of the vote is chargeable to the Department of Immigration and Colonization, because that department formerly collected the samples. However, when the exhibition branch was taken over by the Department of Trade and Commerce this work was transferred and remained chargeable to immigration. I discussed the matter with my colleague, the acting minister (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton), to decide if it was advisable for us to continue to collect these samples, for use at state fairs and on the continent. We concluded that these exhibitions had a double value. They have a general advertising value to Canada. They advertise the Dominion, whether a man be interested in Canada from a tourist standpoint, from the standpoint of an investor or as an immigrant. It is quite possible that when the conference is held with the provinces as to the taking over of immigration the existing service may be continued. It may be that the acting minister may offer to continue to do this work for the provinces. It would be difficult for the general exhibition branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce to get along without this service, whether it is voted for the Department of Immigration and Colonization or for the Department of Trade and Commerce. If there is a saving to be effected as a result of a conference between the minister and the provincial authorities I can assure the committee that I shall be glad to reduce the vote if the result of the conference warrants such action.

911223,ca.proc.d.1930-05-29.20.39,1930-05-29,3e478f06-ec31-4aa2-afb1-2c41dbd6f925,ca.m.9413,Mr. MALCOLM:,Minister of Trade and Commerce,DEPARTMENT OP TRADE AND COMMERCE,,,In reply to my hon.

friend I would say that the point of course is important in trade, but it is hardly relevant to this item. The trade commissioners of Canada are not charged with any duties such as he describes. Their job is to sell Canadian products. He is complaining about a condition which exists whereby continental manufacturers take advantage of the British preference by shipping via Great Britain. I think my hon. friend knows that we have a clause in our customs tariff which compels the man shipping goods under the British preference to take an affidavit to the effect that the goods are 50 per cent British content to enjoy the preference. That is purely a matter for the customs department.

My hon. friend wished to know something about the contributions we make to the International Customs Tariff Bureau. The International Customs Tariff Bureau at Brussels was founded as the result of a convention, signed at Brussels on July 5, 1890, by thirty-nine countries, including Canada. The purpose of the bureau is to translate and distribute, to the various states supporting it, the customs tariffs of the world, with amendments thereto which may be enacted from time to time. To maintain this bureau countries are classified according to their respective volumes of trade and assessed accordingly. At the outset Canada was placed in the third class, for which the contribution was $600. In 1929 Canada, on account of her increased trade, was advanced to the first class, and the Canadian contribution was raised to about $1,319. This amount was increased by 10 per cent, to provide for the superannuation of the few bureau employees. This item is to provide for the translation of the customs tariffs of the world, so that we may have them in our own language. '

911248,ca.proc.d.1930-05-29.23.2,1930-05-29,bec983fd-5d93-4fb8-b921-3a1d702cbebd,ca.m.3148,Mr. GARLAND (Bow River):,,DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE,,,"When the

committee rose a moment ago I was stating that up to this time I had not been unduly alarmed about this situation. However, I find information coming forward, the authenticity of which I cannot vouch for, and I find myself in the same position as the minister. There appears to be a strong belief that in a great section of Russia there has been instituted what might be called a revolution in agricultural operations. I am informed that five years ago some three hundred mechanics were sent from that country to Cleveland and other cities in the United States to study the construction and repairing of tractors. These men returned to Russia and established schools for education in the use of tractors for farming purposes. I am informed that at the beginning of this year there were some 2,000,000 households-that is a unit used as the standard in agricultural matters-in Russia who were under this collectivized system of agriculture. I am informed that on April 1 of this year there were some 14,000,000 households in the scheme, and from 54 to 64 per cent of the tilled land is now alleged to be collectivized. Collectivizing means the organizing of the

country into artels, under the guidance of a peasant committee. Upon that committee is a representative of the Soviet government, a farming expert and an expert accountant. All this appears to have commenced about eighteen months or two years ago with the first experiment being held on a farm which was called the giant farm, under the management of a man named Yourkin. This farm was operated so successfully that the Soviet government became interested and attempted a compulsory organization of the peasants. That was subsequently abandoned as not being the best type of organization, it being found that men who were forced to join were guilty of sabotage or else refused to work. The result was that this scheme was put upon a voluntary basis, and I am informed that the change met with instantaneous success.
I have obtained most of my information from an article which appeared in an English paper known as The New Leader. The article in part reads as follows:
With anything like fair weather, it seems quite possible that the Russian grain crop this coming year will go over the top with a surplus to shake the markets of the world.

This has not been without effort and considerable cost. Yesterday, under my window, marched to the sound of a band the ranks of 1.500 Moscow students, mobilized out to organize farm collectives. The upper two classes of all the agricultural colleges in the land, and the upper class of all agricultural high schools, are being hurled in this first week of March from their desks into the rural districts. Some months ago they were preceded by 25.000 factory workers, the most skilled and the best organizers. The young communist league of the ward of Moscow, where I live, has adopted a township to the north of Moscow, and has sent out hundreds of its chosen youth to organize work in the collectives there.

For the seed collection is only the first sign of success. Now the program of work must be organized, fitting the backward individualist peasants into modern grain production on the factory system. Methods of accounting must, be set up. so that each peasant knows his tasks and his share of the harvest, and sees that he is treated equally with his neighbours. Every piece of farm machinery of every kind in Russia must be got out of -warehouse to the soil in the place where it is most needed.
This gigantic job is being done in the first few weeks of March for more than half the entire peasantry of Russia.

The figures at the end of that month were that 14,000,000 households were enrolled in this single collectivized area and divided in turn into small subdistricts called artels. The organization is one of the most amazingly comprehensive and intelligently conducted I have ever heard of, and far exceeds my wildest dreams of a cooperative commonwealth. I say to the minister that if this
Supply-Trade and Commerce

thing is only one-tenth successful, it will mean that Russia will again be a tremendous factor in the markets of the world. We cannot prevent that, but we should know about it from authoritative sources which cannot be questioned. As I said at the outset, we are going entirely upon articles, some emanating from Russia, others from visitors to Russia and others from possibly guesswork, but I have two or three of these articles under my hand, and they all tell the same story; they all talk of this great scheme. For exemiple, the Labour News, printed in Washington, D.C., says at page 6 of the issue of Saturday, April 5:

The harvest this year in Russia will be the most historic harvest that ever occurred since the prehistoric harvest when man first learned to cast seed on the soil for his food. The harvest this year ushers in a new form of farming, which differs so completely from the old that it must either fail in famine, or begin the farm revolution the world over. To-day the latter alternative seems likely.

The 30 days from January 20 to February 20 of this winter saw a revolution in Russia compared with which the ten days that shook the world was a mere bagatelle. In those 30 days 40 per cent of all Russia's peasants joined collectives, throwing land, horses and implements, into a common pot and planning together for ploughing and sowing. On January 20 only 17 per cent had joined the collectives; by February 20 it was 59 per cent. On January 20, only 55 per cent of the horses were yet collectives; on February 20 it was 44 per cent.

I am informed there are ten or eleven million work animals in the collectivized area, and out of that number more than 8,000,000 are now pooled in the common pot that is spoken of in this article. The article continues :

But how will these collective farms plough? What kind of a harvest will they get? Can fourteen million individual households be merged in one month into a factory form of farming-mass production of grain? That is the number that have joined collectives. The first answer came on March 1, when it was shown that collectives had brought into their central barn the staggering total of 130 million bushels of grain, which they were busy exchanging for cleaned and selected seed of the Department of Agriculture. This fact made it possible for the state to release nearly an equal amount from its reserves to give seed to regions where last year the crop failed.

This is. however, only the beginning. Fourteen million households must be listed on a working schedule, assigned their jobs each day under elected field managers. All implements in warehouses must be rushed to the fields; all local implements must be repaired. To help in this fight 25,000 of the skilled and organized factory workers have been hurled into the villages for the past three months, assisted by 100.000 disciplined red army men. They are followed now by a mobilization of 90 per cent of the farm experts of the nation.

It is most interesting to note that all these stories carry the same basic facts, namely, that the agricultural scientists of Russia are being mobilized and thrown into this tremendous scheme. This man Yourkin, of whom I spoke earlier, was a man who studied this idea on the Campbell farm. Campbell who has the greatest single farm in the United States, at that time the greatest single farm in the world, was taken to Russia and he there gave them information regarding the operation of a gigantic farm of this kind. Some two years ago Yourkin took over the operation of the first experiment of this kind. The description of that is as follows:

Last year Yourkin was director of the Gigant, the biggest farm in the world, three times as big, as Campbell's. This year he has a job which completely dwarfs last year's: he is managing the farming of half Russia. Over

column2: 000 acres of farmland in Russia have come during the past winter under collectivization. This is the farm that Yourkin manages!

column1: The total wheat acreage in western Russia at the present time is 24,000,000 acres. In this we have a suggestion of collective operation of

column2: 000 acres. In no manner does this mean that acreage will be sown to wheat, but I am informed that the most intelligently organized areas are in the best wheat districts of Russia. I do not want to suggest to the committee that we should become unduly alarmed about this situation, although frankly, I am alarmed about it; but I say that we should be in a position to secure accurate information, and I would urge upon the minister, with all the earnestness I can command, that he undertake in some way to see that Canada has that information which is so vital to her, and that we have it in a way and from a source that cannot be questioned. As to how he can get that information I do not know, and I would not dare to venture any particular or specific suggestion; but it occurs to me that he has in Canada organizations now operating in agriculture, some of which would be glad to cooperate with him in this matter. If any means could be found whereby he could send an agent or secure an agent being sent from this country for the purpose of finding out all about this scheme, he would be only doing his duty. I am sorry we have no definite information about it. I realize that is because we cut off trade relations with Russia some years ago.

column1: I am not going to argue at the moment that those relations should be restored. Personally I feel they should be; I think it would be in the trade interests of Canada that they be restored under certain restrictions with regard to propaganda. We are missing a lot of good business by not restoring those trade relations.

Relations between the two countries would be better if trade relations were restored, but the thing of chief importance to me at the moment is the possibility of this tremendous volume of wheat being suddenly thrown on the markets of the world to their complete demoralization. That would be bad enough, but to have it happen without forewarning would be disastrous to western Canada and a very serious matter to the whole of Canada. If we are forewarned, we shall be prepared for the catastrophe, mentally, if not otherwise. We may not be able to take any direct steps to offset it, but I feel we are at least entitled to accurate information as to the condition of affairs in Russia.

friend I would like very much to be able to Secure accurate information as to what is being done in every country in the world, if that were possible; but in the case of Russia I believe he will agree with me that when one gets an optimistic statement from Russia, one can never tell whether it is propaganda or a bear attack on the market. Anybody who has followed the wheat market in Liverpool will recall that on more than one occasion the Liverpool market was brought down several shillings a quarter on account of information from Russia. The cry of ""wolf!"" has gone out so often I have Ceased to be alarmed about the 200,000,000 acres of which my hon. friend has spoken. The most authoritative statements that I have heard made about Russia, or rather, statements made by men whose judgment is, I think conservative and reliable, are to the effect that Russia has to some extent entered on the venture which my hon. friend points out, namely, industrialized agriculture. Having failed deplorably in the operation of her industry to attain any mass production, she seems to have now turned her endeavours to industrialized agriculture.

We are not exercised over the marketing of wheat because we have no control over wheat. The pool in this country sells its own wheat.

and it controls 60 per cent of Canada's crop. The rest of the crop is sold when in the opinion of the owners of the wheat the price is advantageous. I defy any hon. gentleman to say that he can represent Canada in Liverpool and can persuade any miller to buy wheat on any other basis than the day's prevailing price for the grade of a Canadian certificate. The market is so well established that I do not think anybody could persuade the buyer to pay a cent more for a grade that he wanted or to buy a grade that he did not want. We have looked into this situation. There are countries where our trade commissioners have done everything possible to assist, and have cooperated with the agents of the pool; but those countries have not the great buying power of Britain. We are interested in the marketing of anything where we can help, but wheat is a commodity in which it is particularly hard for us to be of active assistance because the owner sells only at the moment he thinks the price is as high as he can obtain.

As to the Russian situation, two things have been pointed out by members who have spoken; namely that Russia is likely to grow a lot more wheat, and that- the Russian people are raising their standard of living. I think everybody realizes that in the days before the war when Russia produced and exported a considerable quantity of wheat she was not a large consumer of her best grades. Now we are told Russia will be a very substantial consumer of those grades. These statements must be judged one in relation to the other. I am informed there will be some Russian wheat come out of northern Russia, and I am told also that there will be a market in southern Russia for as much wheat as northern Russia will export. As a matter of fact, of nineteen boats in all that came from Russia to Canada with coal or pulpwood, sixteen were chartered to take wheat back to Mediterranean ports.

We have here a coal which comes as a result of a very great improvement in Soviet mining conditions and scientific treatment of that product. These people have set for themselves the mark of 300,000,000 tons as a yearly output, and judging from the progress they have made in the last few years it is not unlikely they will reach that enormous output within a short time. This coal may be considered a by-product of anthracite coal. May I point out to the minister that when the first cargoes of Russian anthracite coal came out they consisted of totally unprepared run-of-mine anthracite, and it proved to be a fine fuel. As analysis proved, it is superior to any anthracite of which I am aware, and in that statement I include the anthracite from Scotland, Wales and the United States. It is higher in fixed carbon and lower in ash than the anthracite coal produced to-day in any of those countries, or any such coal which has been mined in those countries within the last twenty years. Last year the coal came out sized egg and nut, and this year it is coming in buckwheat sizes also. This Soviet coal is air washed and is beautifully polished, and entirely free from dust or other impurities. If not air washed it would be a waste product and would be thrown on the dump. It is brought out under a guarantee rate of freight not exceeding 12 shillings a ton with a guarantee to the importers that if the freight goes up to 14, 18 or 20 shillings the exporters will bear the difference between 12 shillings and any advance in freight rates up to 20 shillings per ton. 911313,ca.proc.d.1930-05-29.23.67,1930-05-29,676d5632-265e-4f97-8979-b4ae2f9dc8c8,ca.m.9700,Mr. FANSHER (Last Mountain):,,DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE,,,It is quite all right to be interested in the sale of manufactured products; several million dollars worth of manufactured products go to Great Britain and to Russia from Canada. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said a few moments ago that we would have to take

something in return if we exported to Russia, and the Minister of Finance has made that statement several times during the course of this session. If that be true-and no one doubts it-of necessity we must take more goods from Great Britain. That is absolutely necessary if we expect Great Britain to take from 300,000,000 to 350,000,000 bushels of our wheat to relieve the Canadian market. We must take that much in goods from Great Britain.

I do not wish to delay the committee, but I could give statistics to show that up until the last few months we were taking less than half the amount of goods from Great Britain that would compensate for this amount of wheat. That balance of trade must be looked into. The more we pry the foreign markets open for manufactured goods the more we will have to take in return to pay for those goods, and it is just a question of whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce is going to interest himself in the marketing of our wheat as to whether our next crop will be in any better position than the last one.

I do hope he will seriously consider the remarks of the hon. members I previously mentioned and interest himself in finding out the Russian situation, and interest himself very seriously in seeing what can be done in regard to the marketing of our wheat because it will not find its own market any more; it must be merchandised. When Great Britain has come to the place where she has to resort to bartering, trading her goods for other goods, we must be up and doing in order to get in on that market. The situation is too serious to pass over.

911338,ca.proc.d.1930-05-29.23.92,1930-05-29,3e478f06-ec31-4aa2-afb1-2c41dbd6f925,ca.m.9413,Mr. MALCOLM:,Minister of Trade and Commerce,DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE,,,Will my hon. friend allow me to finish my explanation? Owing to the development on the north shore and the desire of the people on the south shore to take advantage, by way of opportunities for employment and the sale of merchandise, of the development work of the large paper companies that were going in, we were approached by boards of trade or received communications asking us to institute a good service. We had wanted to get commodities from New Brunswick and Nova Scotia more cheaply into northern Quebec in order to give the maritime provinces an opportunity to compete. There are no railways and no good roads through this rapidly developing area and the people are entirely dependent on water service. I had been approached by various people who had little auxiliary schooners like some of the vessels my hon. friend speaks of, to grant a subsidy. I think we had in all four or five appeals for subsidies. During last session I had to provide for a service with good boats across the St. Lawrence and on up to the various points of call. I shall be very frank with my hon. friend as to the Clarke Steamship Company, before I tell him how this amalgamation was brought about. This is the first service in which I have had anything to do with the Clarke Steamship Company which is affiliated with the other companies in this service. The other services they have are the Quebec, Montreal and Gaspe service for which they built a splendid boat called the New Northland, for which service they got $60,000 a year. They extended that to Comerbrook.

911342,ca.proc.d.1930-05-29.23.96,1930-05-29,3e478f06-ec31-4aa2-afb1-2c41dbd6f925,ca.m.9413,Mr. MALCOLM:,Minister of Trade and Commerce,DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE,,,My hon. friend must allow 10 per cent for depreciation and maintenance. These services were installed before I came to the department, and had been in existence for a number of years. There is also the Quebec and Harrington service, carried on by the North Shore and the Voyageur. That is an $85,000 subsidy. The service is extended to Comerbrook fortnightly. Then there is the Murray Bay and north shore winter service, for $32,500. On this service a good deal of money was lost because of ice conditions. I consulted the people who were performing these indifferent services, and asked them whether they could make an amalgamation of the various interests and provide a high class boat which would cost about $250,000, also using the boats that are there at the present time. I suggested that if they would provide an adequate service, and the province of Quebec would pay half of the cost, as it was primarily a business of the province of Quebec, although we were interested in giving Ontario, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia products an opportunity with proper facilities to get into that area, I would consider a term contract. That was the proposition I made to the various interests in the lower St. Lawrence. Mr. Clarke was interested and so were a number of others. I left the matter with those interested to see what could be worked out. They worked out a service and after considerable bartering, we finally agreed that we would pay half of this service if the provincial government would pay half.

The representations made by the hon. member for Fort William do not take into account what is given by way of service. The services are all increased in frequency. The new service to be performed by the Lower St. Lawrence Transportation Company replaces the following services:
column2: Rimouski, Bersimis and Pointe aux Outardes; Rimouski, Pointe aux Outardes and Trinity Bay; Matane, Trinity Bay and Seven Islands.

column1: The Manicouagan will make three trips a week instead of two, and will be remodelled and improved.

On the Rimouski, Pointe aux Outardes and Trinity Bay route, there is the steamer Mayita. This was formerly operated by the Rimouski-Saguenay Navigation company under subsidy, between Rimouski and Pointe aux Outardes only. The Mayita will make three trips a week instead of two, will

perform a regular service to north shore ports as far east as Trinity Bay, and will be replaced on the opening of navigation in 1931 by a new ship with a speed of from eleven to fourteen knots.

On the Matane, Trinity bay and Seven islands route, there was no subsidized service formerly, ibut applications for subsidy have been received frequently in past years from the Heppell Transportation company, the St. Regis Paper company, La Cie de Commerce Maritime de Matane, the Quebec and St. Lawrence Navigation company and Capt. Theodore Piuze.
The Heppell transportation company and the Rimouski-Saguenay Navigation company, have been absorbed by the new Lower St. Lawrence Transportation company.

We have had other applications for the service between the north and south shores from various people. When I took this step I can assure my hon. friend that I was acting much in my own interests, to relieve the pressure from people who wa'ntqd subsidies. There were many small services, and there were many requests for more. I can assure my hon. friend that the contract which was drawn up with the Lower St. Lawrence navigation company is dependent on the vote being passed by this house. If parliament does not vote the money, it cannot be paid. I do submit, however, that the provincial government went carefully into the matter. My hon. friend said that the vote was opposed in the provincial house; I did not know that. I know that the subsidy was to be 50 per cent provincial and 50 per cent federal. I contend, after having looked into the matter very carefully, considering the service they are called upon to perform they will not make much money out of the subsidy they are receiving. My hon. friend also said that someone had offered to perform this service for $10,000. We have had other applications for services between the north and the south shores, from $10,000 down to $5,000. The Des Monts company has just one boat the Savoy. Others who offered to perform the service had no steamer at all, nothing but a schooner.

The Clarke Steamship Company had some interest at the lower St. Lawrence. If my hon. friend will look at the map, he will see that this service crosses from the south shore of the St. Lawrence to the north shore, giving a service to a great many ports on the upper St. Lawrence, which is already served by the Clarke Steamship Company by one of their other ships. I am not a great believer in vested rights, but we have given to the Clarke Steamship Company the service on the north shore, and the Clarke Steamship Company will lose by reason of the competition of this service from the south shore. The service is a great convenience to the travelling public who otherwise would have to go to Quebec and take the boat down the St. Lawrence, or go across to some other point and take the service existing there. I am quite prepared to say to my hon. friend that the interested parties were well approached and had been asked to try to form one amalgamation in the lower St. Lawrence, because I wanted to have one strong company formed and the service put in the hands of those who would put on good boats. We have had people applying for the service who had only an auxiliary schooner. We had applications from people who were not in the transportation business at all. I may say to my hon. friend that the demands the department is making on the Lower St. Lawrence Navigation Company will entail an expenditure on the existing boats of about $35,000 or $40,000, with a 50 per cent greater frequency of service. The existing boats will be scrapped next year

extensive installation of conveying and mailhandling machinery the department endeavoured to obtain standard Canadian manufactured equipment, flexible in construction and noiseless in operation. Not only have the desired results been obtained, but the installation has been completed at a saving of not less than $90,000 as compared with the cost of American stock conveyors previously purchased by the department. The work was let by public tender from time to time during the last four or five years. As regards efficiency of operation it may be mentioned that in the large postal terminal in Toronto, where the installation includes about 3,000 feet of conveyor in daily operation, there has not been 2419-181
a single delay due to mechanical causes since this equipment has been put in.

The use of the patents covered by this vote was obtained at a minimum charge, and the related equipment is of a type which is not duplicated elsewhere in postal work.
